etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English amounten (“to mount up to, come up to, signify”), from Old French amonter (“to amount to”), from amont, amunt (“uphill, upward”), from the prepositional phrase a mont (“toward or to a mountain or heap”), from Latin ad montem, from ad (“to”) + montem, accusative of mons (“mountain”).

definitions.definition: The total, aggregate or sum of material (not applicable to discrete numbers or units or items in standard English).

quote.citation: 2013 July 26, Leo Hickman, “How algorithms rule the world”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 7, page 26:
quote.text: The use of algorithms in policing is one example of their increasing influence on our lives. […] who, if anyone, is policing their use[?] Such concerns were sharpened further by the continuing revelations about how the US National Security Agency (NSA) has been using algorithms to help it interpret the colossal amounts of data it has collected from its covert dragnet of international telecommunications.

definitions.definition: (nonstandard, sometimes proscribed) The number (the sum) of elements in a set.

quote.citation: 2001, Gisella Gori, Towards an EU right to education, page 195:
quote.text: The final amount of students who have participated to mobility for the period 1995-1999 is held to be around 460 000.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, followed by to) To total or evaluate.
(intransitive, followed by to) To be the tantamount to; to reach up to the level of.
(obsolete, intransitive) To go up; to ascend.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto X”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 54:
quote.text: So up he rose, and thence amounted straight.
